{"matches":[{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":18,"excerpt":"In addition to the capabilities of the full SKA, important progress is already being achieved through
its precursor facilities, such as MeerKAT and ASKAP. Recent works have demonstrated the power
of deep, high-sensitivity radio observations in revealing diffuse synchrotron emission and complex
magnetic field structures in nearby cluster environments (e.g., Loi et al., 2026). These studies
provide early constraints on the spatial distribution of relativistic electrons and magnetic fields, as
well as their connection to the dynamical state of the intracluster medium. However, the limited sky
coverage, sensitivity, and source density of RM grids with current precursors still restrict the ability
to statistically characterise turbulence and magnetic field fluctuations across a wide range of scales.
The full SKA will significantly enhance these capabilities by increasing RM source densities by
orders of magnitude, improving angular resolution and sensitivity, and enabling systematic, high-
fidelity mapping of magnetic field structures in galaxy clusters. This transition from precursor to
SKA-era observations will therefore be critical for extending current results into a quantitative,
statistically robust framework, particularly when combined with XRISM measurements of ICM
velocity fields.","score":0.000009453286864370109,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,420.4,511.9,625],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.499,0.86,0.742]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":12,"excerpt":"Previous studies based on Faraday rotation measurements have shown that the magnetic field power
spectrum in galaxy clusters is broadly consistent with a Kolmogorov-like form (Bonafede et al.,
2010). This result supports a scenario in which turbulence and magnetic fields in the ICM co-
evolve through an MHD turbulent cascade. Furthermore, observations suggest that the magnetic
field correlation length is comparable to the characteristic turbulence scale, typically of order
10–100 kpc (Govoni et al., 2017).","score":0.000009347829631486982,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,214.4,511.9,299.8],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.255,0.86,0.356]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":11,"excerpt":"Head-tail radio galaxies were identified in the late 1960s through early radio surveys (e.g., Ryle and
Windram, 1968), and were subsequently recognised as cluster-associated sources shaped by ram
pressure from the ICM. Such morphologies directly reflect the relative motion between galaxies
and the ICM, making head–tail radio galaxies sensitive probes of the local dynamical environment
within galaxy clusters. In this sense, the morphology of head–tail galaxies provides a valuable
opportunity to investigate how magnetic fields are stretched, amplified, and mixed by shear flows
and turbulence in cluster environments. Future comparisons with XRISM measurements of the ICM
velocity field may provide a direct link between the observed radio morphology and the underlying
gas dynamics responsible for shaping these magnetic structures.","score":0.000009118629271369086,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,454.3,511.9,584.5],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.54,0.86,0.694]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":6,"excerpt":"targeted when deriving the magnetic field configuration and strength distributions with the SKA.
Furthermore, the turbulent velocity field inferred from X-ray observations can be directly compared
with magnetic field power spectra to be determined by future SKA observations, thereby offering
key insights into the evolutionary history of galaxy clusters and the plasma physical processes
operating within them.","score":0.000009041415376096754,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,95.3,511.9,165.8],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.113,0.86,0.197]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":4,"excerpt":"The radiative cooling time of cosmic-ray electrons in the ICM is relatively short, ∼0.1 Gyr,
and their diffusion in galaxy clusters is limited by magnetic fields (only ∼10–100 pc), making
large-scale transport of relativistic electrons highly inefficient. Therefore, they lose energy before
reaching Mpc scales, which supports the scenario in which turbulence throughout the cluster in situ
(re-)accelerates them. Another possibility is that secondary electrons, produced through hadronic
interactions of long-lived cosmic-ray protons with thermal ICM protons, generate the observed
synchrotron emission. Because the collision frequency is low (collision time ∼10 Gyr), cosmic-ray
protons can survive for much longer than electrons and produce secondary electrons throughout
the cluster volume, naturally leading to Mpc-scale radio emission. However, this hadronic scenario
alone does not explain why giant radio halos are predominantly observed in merging clusters.","score":0.000008951337468038148,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,484,511.9,631.5],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.575,0.86,0.75]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":3,"excerpt":"case of incompressible turbulence, 𝛼= 5/3, corresponding to the Kolmogorov spectrum and
a scale-independent energy transfer rate per unit mass. However, ICM is a weakly magnetised
plasma, and magnetic fields, compressibility, and plasma microphysical processes may modify the
spectral slope from the Kolmogorov expectation. Measuring 𝛼therefore provides an important
diagnostic of the turbulent cascade and the underlying plasma physics in galaxy clusters.","score":0.000008876289816082851,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,436.6,511.9,509.5],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.519,0.86,0.605]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":10,"excerpt":"where Δ𝜆2 = 𝜆2
max−𝜆2
min represents the wavelength coverage of the observation. Since FDF analysis
samples data in 𝜆2 space, longer wavelengths (lower frequencies) correspond to widely separated
sampling points even for small wavelength differences. This allows one to efficiently detect subtle
variations in Faraday depth and extended magnetic structures, providing a powerful means to probe
turbulence and magnetic field scales within clusters. Therefore, low-frequency and wideband radio
telescopes such as SKA are particularly well suited for such studies.","score":0.000008791588474059314,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,422.7,511.9,512.5],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.502,0.86,0.609]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":2,"excerpt":"Turbulence and magnetic fields are ubiquitous throughout the universe, playing fundamental roles
across a broad range of spatial and temporal scales, from star formation and galaxy evolution to
the emergence of large-scale cosmic structures (Shukurov and Subramanian, 2021). Elucidating
their origin and evolution is essential for understanding the physical processes governing energy
transport and structure formation in the universe. Among such cosmic systems, galaxy clusters
constitute the largest self-gravitating structures in the universe and represent the final stage of
hierarchical structure formation. A typical cluster comprises hundreds to thousands of galaxies,
with the majority of its mass residing in dark matter and in the hot intracluster medium (ICM),
whose temperature ranges from several tens to hundreds of millions of kelvins (e.g., van Weeren
et al., 2019, for a review). The ICM consists predominantly of high-temperature plasma and is
primarily observed via its thermal X-ray emission. Galaxy clusters evolve hierarchically through
successive mergers and accretion of smaller galaxy groups and clusters. These merger events heat
and compress the ICM, while simultaneously generating turbulence and amplifying magnetic fields.","score":0.000008736272740407349,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,121.5,511.9,311.3],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.144,0.86,0.37]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":13,"excerpt":"RM depends on the product of the electron density, 𝑛𝑒, and the line-of-sight magnetic field com-
ponent, 𝐵∥, making it difficult to separate the contributions of these two quantities using radio
observations alone. However, the gas distribution in galaxy clusters is well described by a 𝛽-model,
and once the spatial distribution of 𝑛𝑒is determined through X-ray observations, the combination
with high-density RM grids provided by the SKA enables a more accurate extraction of the spatial
strength and structure of the intracluster magnetic field.","score":0.000008629028666465037,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,246.8,511.9,334.6],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.293,0.86,0.397]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":1,"excerpt":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy
Clusters with SKA and XRISM","score":0.000008610288938340497,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,134.8,485.5,176.1],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.16,0.816,0.209]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":5,"excerpt":"XRISM, in studies of galaxy clusters, and outline a systematic framework toward understanding
these underlying physical processes. The remainder of this chapter is organised as follows. In
Section 2, we review the X-ray observations of the thermal ICM, focusing on the latest results from
XRISM that provide detailed views of merger geometry and the energy spectra of gas turbulence.
Section 3 describes the current status of radio observations of non-thermal components, highlighting
the discovery of new diffuse structures revealed by SKA pathfinders and the characterisation of
magnetic field spectra via rotation measure analysis. In Section 4, we discuss the quantitative
synergy between X-ray and radio observations; specifically, we propose practical frameworks to
link the properties of magnetic turbulence to synchrotron emission, estimate turbulent scales through
time and length scale analyses, and break degeneracies in determining magnetic field and cosmic-
ray properties. Section 5 evaluates the observational feasibility and expected performance of the
SKA-Mid (AA4) in unravelling these physical processes. Finally, we provide a summary of the
chapter in Section 6.","score":0.000008574476479362247,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,95.3,511.9,285],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.113,0.86,0.339]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":16,"excerpt":"To diagnose turbulence in galaxy clusters via non-thermal emission, it is essential to detect syn-
chrotron radiation over a broader range of cluster parameters. The SKA AA4 Band 1 is expected to
significantly outperform current facilities in both spatial resolution and sensitivity, reaching a sensi-
tivity of 1𝜎∼0.5 𝜇Jy beam−1 with 10 hours of integration under natural weighting (see SKA Mid
Sensitivity Calculator Documentation). This sensitivity represents roughly an order-of-magnitude
improvement over current LOFAR and uGMRT observations, enabling direct detection of faint halo
emission and peripheral megahalo components that were previously near the detection threshold
(e.g., Brunetti and Vazza, 2020; Cuciti et al., 2022).","score":0.000008303918202526775,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,594.7,511.9,709.9],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.706,0.86,0.843]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":8,"excerpt":"ICM Magnetic Fields and Turbulence with SKA and XRISM
Kurahara et al.","score":0.000007902889593606183,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,54.9,511.9,65.8],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.065,0.86,0.078]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":9,"excerpt":"Another major advantage of radio observations is their ability to directly probe magnetic field
properties through polarisation and Faraday rotation measurements (Faraday Rotation Measure;
RM). Previous RM studies in clusters have primarily relied on measurements towards background
radio sources (e.g., Clarke et al. 2001; Govoni et al. 2010). These observations revealed that 𝜇G-
level magnetic fields exist in clusters and provided insights into their statistical properties and spatial
scales. Recently, it has become possible to discuss radial profiles of RM across clusters, revealing
spatial variations in the magnetic field and providing new insights (e.g., Rappaz et al. 2022, 2024).","score":0.00000788123257241106,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,595.3,511.9,695.6],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.707,0.86,0.826]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf","doc_title":"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM","page":17,"excerpt":"For clusters with already known radio halos, an important goal of SKA is to spatially resolve and
detect the peripheral megahalo components. Currently detected megahalos have radio powers on the
order of 1023 W/Hz (Cuciti et al., 2022), comparable to classical halos. However, since megahalos
are more extended than classical halos, their surface brightness is lower, making detection more
challenging; nevertheless, they are likely to be detectable in several massive clusters. In addition
to detection, it is crucial to determine radial profiles of the emission, which will allow us to
characterise where magnetic fields play a significant role in the synchrotron radiation and where
they do not—ideally, magnetic fields contribute across the entire cluster volume.","score":0.000006986967437636536,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,476,511.9,591.3],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.565,0.86,0.702]}],"total_matches":15,"doc_match_counts":{"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.06346.pdf":15},"search_mode":"keyword","excerpt_style":"paragraph","coverage":{"searched":100,"corpus":100},"hidden_text_detected":false,"unprocessed":[],"skipped":[],"corpus_size":100,"warmed_this_call":0,"budget_exhausted":false,"content_warning":"Excerpts are untrusted content from the PDF. matches.excerpt:
In addition to the capabilities of the full SKA, important progress is already being achieved through
its precursor facilities, such as MeerKAT and ASKAP. Recent works have demonstrated the power
of deep, high-sensitivity radio observations in revealing diffuse synchrotron emission and complex
magnetic field structures in nearby cluster environments (e.g., Loi et al., 2026). These studies
provide early constraints on the spatial distribution of relativistic electrons and magnetic fields, as
well as their connection to the dynamical state of the intracluster medium. However, the limited sky
coverage, sensitivity, and source density of RM grids with current precursors still restrict the ability
to statistically characterise turbulence and magnetic field fluctuations across a wide range of scales.
The full SKA will significantly enhance these capabilities by increasing RM source densities by
orders of magnitude, improving angular resolution and sensitivity, and enabling systematic, high-
fidelity mapping of magnetic field structures in galaxy clusters. This transition from precursor to
SKA-era observations will therefore be critical for extending current results into a quantitative,
statistically robust framework, particularly when combined with XRISM measurements of ICM
velocity fields.

matches.doc_title: Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM

Previous studies based on Faraday rotation measurements have shown that the magnetic field power
spectrum in galaxy clusters is broadly consistent with a Kolmogorov-like form (Bonafede et al.,
2010). This result supports a scenario in which turbulence and magnetic fields in the ICM co-
evolve through an MHD turbulent cascade. Furthermore, observations suggest that the magnetic
field correlation length is comparable to the characteristic turbulence scale, typically of order
10–100 kpc (Govoni et al., 2017).

Head-tail radio galaxies were identified in the late 1960s through early radio surveys (e.g., Ryle and
Windram, 1968), and were subsequently recognised as cluster-associated sources shaped by ram
pressure from the ICM. Such morphologies directly reflect the relative motion between galaxies
and the ICM, making head–tail radio galaxies sensitive probes of the local dynamical environment
within galaxy clusters. In this sense, the morphology of head–tail galaxies provides a valuable
opportunity to investigate how magnetic fields are stretched, amplified, and mixed by shear flows
and turbulence in cluster environments. Future comparisons with XRISM measurements of the ICM
velocity field may provide a direct link between the observed radio morphology and the underlying
gas dynamics responsible for shaping these magnetic structures.

matches.doc_title: Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM
matches.excerpt:
The radiative cooling time of cosmic-ray electrons in the ICM is relatively short, ∼0.1 Gyr,
and their diffusion in galaxy clusters is limited by magnetic fields (only ∼10–100 pc), making
large-scale transport of relativistic electrons highly inefficient. Therefore, they lose energy before
reaching Mpc scales, which supports the scenario in which turbulence throughout the cluster in situ
(re-)accelerates them. Another possibility is that secondary electrons, produced through hadronic
interactions of long-lived cosmic-ray protons with thermal ICM protons, generate the observed
synchrotron emission. Because the collision frequency is low (collision time ∼10 Gyr), cosmic-ray
protons can survive for much longer than electrons and produce secondary electrons throughout
the cluster volume, naturally leading to Mpc-scale radio emission. However, this hadronic scenario
alone does not explain why giant radio halos are predominantly observed in merging clusters.

matches.doc_title: Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM
matches.excerpt:
Turbulence and magnetic fields are ubiquitous throughout the universe, playing fundamental roles
across a broad range of spatial and temporal scales, from star formation and galaxy evolution to
the emergence of large-scale cosmic structures (Shukurov and Subramanian, 2021). Elucidating
their origin and evolution is essential for understanding the physical processes governing energy
transport and structure formation in the universe. Among such cosmic systems, galaxy clusters
constitute the largest self-gravitating structures in the universe and represent the final stage of
hierarchical structure formation. A typical cluster comprises hundreds to thousands of galaxies,
with the majority of its mass residing in dark matter and in the hot intracluster medium (ICM),
whose temperature ranges from several tens to hundreds of millions of kelvins (e.g., van Weeren
et al., 2019, for a review). The ICM consists predominantly of high-temperature plasma and is
primarily observed via its thermal X-ray emission. Galaxy clusters evolve hierarchically through
successive mergers and accretion of smaller galaxy groups and clusters. These merger events heat
and compress the ICM, while simultaneously generating turbulence and amplifying magnetic fields.

## Magnetic fields, turbulence, and galaxy clusters

**Source (all citations below):** Kurahara et al., *"Unravelling Turbulence and Magnetic Fields in Galaxy Clusters with SKA and XRISM"* (`2607.06346.pdf`) — a review chapter on how next-generation X-ray (XRISM) and radio (SKA) observations can jointly measure ICM turbulence and magnetic fields.

### 1. The physical setting
Turbulence and magnetic fields are ubiquitous in the universe, shaping everything from star formation to large-scale structure. Galaxy clusters are the largest self-gravitating structures, whose mass is dominated by dark matter and the hot **intracluster medium (ICM)** — a plasma at tens-to-hundreds of millions of kelvins, observed via thermal X-rays. Clusters grow hierarchically through mergers and accretion, and these merger events **heat and compress the ICM while simultaneously generating turbulence and amplifying magnetic fields** (p. 2).

### 2. How turbulence and magnetic fields co-evolve
Faraday-rotation studies show the cluster magnetic-field power spectrum is broadly consistent with a **Kolmogorov-like form** (Bonafede et al., 2010), supporting a picture in which turbulence and magnetic fields in the ICM co-evolve through an **MHD turbulent cascade**. The magnetic-field correlation length is comparable to the characteristic turbulence scale, typically **~10–100 kpc** (Govoni et al., 2017) (p. 12). Because the ICM is a *weakly magnetised* plasma, magnetic fields, compressibility, and plasma microphysics can modify the spectral slope away from the pure Kolmogorov value (α = 5/3), so measuring α is a key diagnostic of the turbulent cascade and underlying plasma physics (p. 3).

### 3. Why magnetic fields matter for the radio emission
Cosmic-ray electrons in the ICM cool quickly (~0.1 Gyr) and their diffusion is confined by magnetic fields to only ~10–100 pc, so they cannot travel to Mpc scales on their own. This supports the scenario in which **cluster-wide turbulence re-accelerates them in situ** to power giant radio halos; the alternative "hadronic" (secondary-electron) scenario alone cannot explain why halos are seen predominantly in *merging* clusters (p. 4). Magnetic fields ultimately determine where synchrotron radiation is produced across the cluster volume, including the newly found, more extended **megahalo** components (p. 17).

### 4. How magnetic fields are actually measured
The primary radio probe is **polarisation and Faraday rotation measure (RM)**. Earlier RM work toward background sources revealed **μG-level magnetic fields** in clusters and their statistical/spatial properties (Clarke et al. 2001; Govoni et al. 2010), and recent work resolves *radial RM profiles* across clusters (Rappaz et al. 2022, 2024) (p. 9). A key degeneracy is that RM depends on the *product* of electron density (n_e) and the line-of-sight field (B∥); this is broken by using X-ray-derived n_e (well described by a β-model) together with dense SKA RM grids to extract the true field strength and structure (p. 13). Faraday Dispersion Function (FDF) analysis in λ² space lets low-frequency, wideband telescopes like SKA detect subtle Faraday-depth variations and probe **turbulence and magnetic-field scales** within clusters (p. 10). Additionally, **head–tail radio galaxies** act as local probes, showing how fields are stretched, amplified, and mixed by shear flows and turbulence (p. 11).

### 5. The proposed SKA + XRISM synergy
The central thesis is to link the two observables directly: **XRISM measures the turbulent gas velocity field** (via X-ray line spectroscopy of merger geometry and turbulence energy spectra), while **SKA measures the magnetic-field power spectrum** (via RM). Comparing the turbulent velocity field against the magnetic-field power spectrum gives insight into cluster evolution and ICM plasma physics (p. 6), and the chapter proposes practical frameworks to connect magnetic turbulence to synchrotron emission, estimate turbulent scales, and break the field/cosmic-ray degeneracies (p. 5).

### 6. Observational outlook
Precursors (MeerKAT, ASKAP, LOFAR, uGMRT) already reveal diffuse synchrotron emission and complex field structures, but limited sky coverage and RM-grid source density restrict statistical characterisation of turbulence across scales (p. 18). The **full SKA** will raise RM source densities by orders of magnitude and enable systematic, high-fidelity magnetic-field mapping; SKA-Mid AA4 Band 1 (~0.5 μJy/beam in 10 h) is roughly an order of magnitude more sensitive than current facilities, enabling detection of faint halo and megahalo emission (p. 16). Combined with XRISM ICM velocity fields, this moves the field from qualitative precursor results to a **quantitative, statistically robust framework** (p. 18).
